utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first matter is this: That we are constituted as a Chamber of two, Judge Robinson being absent for urgent personal reasons, which I trust has been communicated to the parties. We cannot, therefore, make any decisions sitting as a Chamber of two, and we can only do so as a Chamber of three. However, given the urgency of matters and the need to get on, we thought it right to sit today in order to hear argument. We will not make a decision until we are fully composed as a Chamber of three, which will be sometime after the 25th of this month. If there's any objection to that course, we will hear it, but otherwise we propose to hear the argument now. Judge Robinson will have access to all materials about this hearing. Mr. Rivkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: We have no objections, Your Honours. Indeed we were informed about this matter in a timely manner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have no objection, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will hear the matter. Those matters, as I understand it, which we are to consider are these: alleged non-compliance by the Republic of Croatia with orders of the Trial Chamber of the 22nd of January and the 4th of February of last year, and then further requests by the Prosecution of the 16th of April and the 19th of July of last year. We have been helpfully provided -- besides all the voluminous materials, we've been helpfully provided with a summary by the Prosecution of the status of the litigation which sets out all the steps in a very comprehensive form. I hope that the Republic have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honour, we do not. I was as disappointed as you, Your Honour. The Registrar's office has evidently adopted a new policy of sending things to us by regular mail. Consequently, the document I think you're referring to arrived in our offices about 9.00 last night Hague time, about 3.00 Washington time. It is quite voluminous, and so we have not yet received the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask the Registry about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The document, say there's no dispute about it, in case there is a misunderstanding, the summary of the binding order is the document I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Yes. We were given that this morning. Evidently there is another quite voluminous filing that was made on December 22nd by the Prosecution summarising its view of the various binding orders and the status of that, and that is the document I was referring to. I was mistaken. I thought that's the one you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We have, as I say, the summary, helpfully setting out the matter. So the parties may take it that we have all the materials. It may be helpful, Mr. Nice, if in as non-contentious a way as possible you could state the Prosecution's position, what you're asking us to do today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First, the absent document. It's unfortunate that the representatives of the State of Croatia don't have that substantial document which, of course, we rely on. My understanding, from the marks on the document as filed, is that it was severed on the embassy as well as on the law firm. So, therefore, if that's right and it was served on the embassy here, they should have been aware of it acting for the state shortly after the time when it was served on the embassy. The document does contain a number of matters of detail and a number of exhibits, some of which may be thought to be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be then that since the respondents haven't had it, if you were to take us to that document and briefly indicate the salient points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can make a preliminary point and indeed sit down. It's a new policy of the Office of the Prosecutor that filings are only ever to be signed by the Senior Trial Attorney. That's somewhat unfair on the people who do the work and doesn't help you know who has actually done the drafting in this case. It won't come as any surprise that the very considerable work that's been put into this exercise has been done by Mr. Scott and having opened the next application in a couple of sentences I will hand over to him. So I will do that straight away. The only thing I desire to make quite plain now, because it hasn't been made plain, I think, to the representatives of the State of Croatia before now, is that in light of the history, we're asking the Chamber not only to make orders which would be very short in their return dates, but we're asking the Chamber effectively to take over and to police the provision of documents, particularly given the time scale. And by that we would invite the Chamber, in due course, to make orders that documents be provided to the Chamber on particular dates and that there be attendance either on that date or very shortly after by the representatives of the state to check whether there has been proper compliance and so that appropriate steps can be taken if there has not been proper compliance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you would ask for orders on all these applications for documents to be supplied by 28 days or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or even less because of the real timetable problems we are suffering and for the period of time these requests have been outstanding, to be followed by timetabled return dates for appearance by the parties so that the matter can be dealt with immediately if provision of documents is anything other than complete and adequate. The only other point I was going to make is that in the long document that apparently has not found its way to the representatives of the State of Croatia, there is some chapter and verse given to what we now know of the involvement of both sides of Hunton and Williams and the State of Croatia in the Kordic defence. That starts at page 40 in the long document. The Chamber will be pleased to know that I have managed to release the underlying documents from any sensitivity, and I'm going to be in a position to provide them almost immediately with full translations to the Defence in this case and, indeed, in due course to the representatives of the State of Croatia. I shan't serve them immediately on the Chamber for this reason: that I will give those representing the defendant, or both defendants, the opportunity to indicate what passages, if anything, they would rather were not seen by the Trial Judges, if there is any sensitivity that they regard as attaching to any such passages. But the material is now available to be served, and therefore we're able to be a little bit more explicit about it. With those few opening observations, I'll hand over to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may make one point before going forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: With respect to the service on the embassy, indeed it is the practice of the registrar to serve things on the embassy of Croatia here in The Hague, as well as send things to us. Unfortunately, when the service sheet indicates that it has also been served upon us, they assume that that has been the case and that therefore they need not also provide us with a copy, and consequently they would have had no reason to provide the document that we're talking about to us, assuming that we had it. And, of course, we had no idea that it existed and so did not know to ask for it. With respect to compliance times, again we believe the Court's law on this is quite clear. Reasonable compliant times must be provided, and we would obviously request the opportunity to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can address us on that in due course. Let us hear briefly, if we could, Mr. Scott, so that the respondents can have an opportunity to deal with the document. If you would just take us to the salient parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court and counsel, I'll try to be brief, Your Honour. I may be slightly more detailed than I might otherwise have been because of the service issue, and I'll try to flush out our position on some of these issues so that counsel can fully respond. It is the case, Your Honour, that considerable effort did go into the preparation of these papers. I say that not expecting any particular response from the Court, only to say that they are as exhaustive and as detailed and as complete as we could possibly make them. I certainly can't say anything terribly new or different this morning but will try to highlight to the Court our basic points and again flush them out to some further extent for counsel. Your Honour, it is our fundamental position here before this Court, and I start with this point and we will probably end with this point, that we come here today, after three years of a continuous series of events, all of which are closely related, in a continuing series of efforts by the Prosecutor's office and by, indeed, this Court, at least two separate Chambers, to obtain Croatia's full and complete compliance with outstanding orders, requests for assistance, and other outstanding matters. It is the Prosecutor's position, Your Honour, that the status of these matters and Croatia's obvious complete and continuing non-compliance is not a matter of an isolated incident or instance here and there but part of a strategy, if you will, part of a campaign, if you will, to resist and delay and obstruct the work of this Tribunal. We set our reasons for that out, our basis for that, Your Honour, in great detail in our papers, and again I'll touch on some of them. Your Honour, we believe it is reasonable for the Court to conclude, and the Prosecutor has concluded, that there are, in fact, substantial documents in existence in the Republic of Croatia that are responsive to our outstanding request and, in fact, indeed the Court's orders. Everything about these investigations today, and this Tribunal is now some years old and there has been some extensive amount of investigation, everything points to the fact that these organisations, these States, these entities, are modern organisations with extensive record-keeping, with extensive archives, with extensive document collections. There is every reason to believe and no reason to believe to the contrary that substantial responsive documents directly relevant to the issues before this Tribunal exist and should be turned over to this Tribunal. To the extent, Your Honours, that some documents are claimed to have been lost or in the meantime destroyed, we submit, Your Honours, that someone, some responsible senior official, should come before this Court, under oath, and make a full accounting concerning those documents. I want to touch on, Your Honour, two important issues in this case that underlie many of our requests or many of our requests touch on to simply flush out the basis for our requests and our concerns. One of these, as the Court knows, is the whole issue of international armed conflict, and indeed the Court heard only yesterday that it is an issue in this case that the Defence does not concede in the slightest, putting the Prosecution in the position of having to prove, as we believe we have and will, the existence of such a conflict for purposes of sustaining our burden of proof. In that regard then, Your Honours, again going back to 1997, the Prosecutor's office has repeatedly sought documents from Croatia related to this issue. It's the Prosecutor's position, Your Honour, that there was, indeed, an international armed conflict relevant to the issues in this case, that is, the conflict in Central Bosnia between the Bosnian Croats or Croats and the Bosniak or Muslim community during the time from approximately late 1991 into early 1994. It's our position, Your Honour, that indeed the most senior officials of the Zagreb government, including former President Tudjman and Defence Minister Susak, were extensively involved with the Bosnian Croat leadership, including such people as Mate Boban and, in fact, indeed, at least one of the accused, Mr. Kordic. This Court has heard to date, since the trial started on the 12th of April, substantial and extensive evidence of this, of Croatia's close relationship and involvement in these matters. Our papers set forth a number of the witnesses who have touched on these matters. I won't take the time to go through it here. We also cite a number of the more directly-relevant exhibits that have come before the Court touching on this. The Court will remember, even in the past several weeks, some of the directly pertinent testimony of such people as Ole Brix Andersen and others who have come before this Court and said, in no uncertain terms, the government of Croatia, the forces of the HV, the Croatian army, the military forces, were involved in Bosnia, including Central Bosnia, and it is, we believe, untenable, Your Honour, for Croatia to have come before this Court for the past three years and denied that involvement. We do not accept that position. In particular, Your Honour, at pages 17, 18, and 19 of our papers, we've spent specific incidents and examples of such involvement, including, for instance -- and I'm just going to cite a couple, Your Honour -- an order on the 12th of April, 1992, from a very senior Croatian army officer, Janko Bobetko, the commander of all HV -- not HVO -- all HV units on the, quote, "southern front" ordering that all HV insignia are to be removed from the fighters, that such fighters will present themselves as volunteer defenders of their homeland. On the 5th of October, 1992, Colonel Blaskic issued a written order that all HV officers in the HVO units be identified. On the 26th of November, 1992, the HVO deputy commander in Zenica, and that is right in Central Bosnia, right in the middle of this case, ordered that HV members present in this region and wearing HV insignia must be warned to take them off. Again as late as the 17th of February, 1994, the U.N. Secretary-General, no less, sends a letter to the Security Council concerning the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia and the removal, the policy or strategy of removing their HV insignia. This Court has heard sworn testimony from Witness A that Croatian army symbols and insignia were seen on troops and equipment in Central Bosnia in early '93 and that Dario Kordic, as a senior official of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian arm of the HDZ party and vice-president of Herceg-Bosna, often travelled to Croatian and was the superior persons who were directly involved in bringing weapons from Croatian. A still confidential witness, Your Honour, to come in the future is expected to testify to extensive contact between the Bosnian-Croat leadership and senior officials of the Zagreb government, including President Tudjman. Another specific example, and I say this again, Your Honour, because Croatia has come for three years and said, "We have no records of this. We have no records of any meetings. We have no records that Mate Boban was in Zagreb meeting with these officials. We have no records that Dario Kordic ever came to Zagreb and met with President Tudjman or Defence Minister Susak." Just as an example, trial Exhibit Z2787 is a photograph of a meeting of a Bosnian-Croat delegation including Kordic and Valenta with President Tudjman in June of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've got this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, if you could take us on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, quickly. Suffice it to say, and again, Your Honour, we set this out in great detail continuing on, and just for the record for the Court and counsel, continuing on to pages 20 to 22 or so of our brief, detailed accounts in support of our position. We think, Your Honour, it is untenable for Croatia to come before the Court and say that relevant documents don't exist. As a further specific issue, Your Honour, one particular event that I'd say probably most people in this Tribunal and certainly this Court is very familiar with at this point is the whole issue of the atrocities in Ahmici. Many of our requests, again dating to three years ago, and I say that, Your Honour, because the Court will recall now from the newspapers that Judge McDonald, in January of 1997, almost to the day, I think the 15th it will be three years from the anniversary date, issued a subpoena to this very same Croatia for many of the very same documents that we have never received, including the documents concerning Ahmici. As recently as May of this year, Your Honour, Croatia filed a response that said it has no documents about Ahmici, whether produced by its own agents, that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that that particular response was, indeed, issued in closed session, and because of the state's concerns, and I would prefer it not be referred to in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We know what the response was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that in mind, Your Honour, it is again incredible to the Prosecution, and we ask the Court to come to a similar conclusion, that there would be no such documents. The record is clear, Your Honour, there was extensive public -- international public outcry about these events in Ahmici by virtually every western government, by the United Nations, by the European Union, et cetera, et cetera, that came directly to bear on President Tudjman and the Zagreb government. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can discuss this, it may be sensible to go into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can go into private session, Your Honour, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whatever it is, yes. Private session will do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 25 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that further background in mind, Your Honour, let me touch upon the status of the outstanding matters and the pending applications. Again, Your Honour, as touched on already, and I'll try not to say this more than again once or twice, but it is of paramount importance for this Court not only to hear but fully understand and appreciate that these events are part of an unbroken string going to January of 1997. Croatia does not appear before this Court for the first time on a first request for these documents but comes here some three years later to the day never having produced many of the documents requested. In fact, even at that time, back in January of 1997, in February of 1997, in hearings, when Croatia's representative disputed the power of the Tribunal at that time to issue a subpoena, nonetheless, at the urging of Judge McDonald, Croatia's representative at that time undertook and made a personal commitment -- made a commitment on behalf of the Croatian government that indeed notwithstanding the technical legal issues about a subpoena or what have you, made a commitment to this Tribunal that those documents would be produced, and, in fact, in reliance on that commitment or to further record that commitment, the Office of the Prosecutor in the Blaskic case, Mr. Harmon, on that same day, drafted a request for assistance, a Rule 29 request asking for the same documents not by subpoena, which was disputed by Croatia, but by a Rule 29 request which they stood in court in front of Judge McDonald and said they would honour and they've never done so. Since we're in public session, Your Honour, I will not go into detail about some of the additional history in the Blaskic case. The Court has our papers and the Court knows and Croatia knows the severe findings that the Blaskic hearing officer made concerning the status of Croatia's compliance in June of 1998, in the most severe and unqualified terms. To make the record clear, Your Honour, unless Croatia say that we're suggesting otherwise, it is the case, and we have always said that after the very severe findings by the Blaskic Chamber in June of 1998, which again this Court has available to it in detail, Croatia did make then a series of some productions between that time and the end of the Blaskic evidence. It's our view and the Court has heard this already; that notwithstanding the production of paper, that Croatia was not and never was in compliance with the orders in that case. It is not simply compliance, Your Honour, to produce a volume of material, most of which is completely non-responsive and irrelevant. It's no secret, Your Honour. I could show up in this Court this afternoon and deliver boxes of material, most of which would be worthless. There have been productions by Croatia. We don't want to suggest that there hasn't been some paper presented to the Prosecutor's Officer. It's our position, Your Honour -- we've assessed that. Mr. Harmon's assessed it. Most of it was completely unresponsive, most of it completely irrelevant. Generously speaking, Your Honour, and I'll ask Mr. Harmon to conclude, but certainly probably the total material was probably not more than a small box, perhaps a printing paper -- Xerox box of material. Mr. Harmon confirms that that's correct. A very small amount of material, given the circumstances of this case and over the time period that these orders have been outstanding. In fact, Your Honour, the net result of Croatia's position, unfortunately and sadly, was through a continuous process of promising compliance, coming before this Court, coming before the Blaskic Chamber, Judge Jorda, now President Jorda, and professing good faith, professing cooperation, in fact producing almost nothing, Croatia succeeded, and it's my view, Your Honour, and I submit to the Court it's not by accident, Croatia succeeded in out-lasting the taking of evidence in the Blaskic case. So that any evidence produced, and in reality no further evidence produced, was too late to put before the Blaskic Trial Chamber. I submit, Your Honour, I'll be so bold to submit, if the Court will allow me, that unless the Court takes stern measures in this case, we fear, the Prosecution fears the same will be true here, and to the extent any documents produced by Croatia, they will be too late. On the 5th of June, 1998, Your Honour, we served, the Prosecutor's Office served a formal request for assistance to Croatia concerning information for Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez. 5th of June 1998, some year and a half ago. No documents ever produced. On the 24th of July, 1998, the Prosecutor's Office applied for a binding order essentially to step into the shoes of the Blaskic order as it then stood. We believed it important, Your Honour, because of concerns in the Blaskic case and because the Kordic case, of course, stands on its own feet in terms of a separate record, to make the same request and have the same order issued in this case, for the very reason that in the unfortunate scenario, which sadly came true, that Croatia would outlast, if you will, the Blaskic trial, the Kordic team would take the baton and continue our efforts to obtain these documents. That is now some almost 18 months ago. No documents produced. Indeed, I'll just mention in passing -- there's a longer quote in our papers, but I'll just mention that when this matter was still before the prior Trial Chamber, Judge Jorda presiding, on the 2nd of September 1998, Judge Jorda, closely familiar with the history in the Blaskic case made this statement on the record: "I appreciate the fact that the Prosecutor has already asked for us, and I know I'm speaking for my colleagues and for the Tribunal as a whole, I'm appreciative of the fact that the country or countries covered by bindings orders will not say that they can escape from orders, and the orders of the Prosecution or Defence has gone about things too late in order to ask for production, and the binding orders here will be issued in the Kordic/Cerkez case," he's referring to, "from the very start of the proceedings, and we intend to make sure that those binding orders are respected specifically in respect of the country covered by the first binding order; that is, Croatia." Let me make the general point, Your Honour, to the extent that on any of these matters, and really this touches on more than one application or one order, to the extent that national security claims are made, let me submit to the Court that in our collective view and experience as a Prosecution team, including Mr. Harmon, generic claims or general abstract claims of alleged national security are far too easy to make, and in many, many instances those claims cannot, in fact, withstand scrutiny, and there's simply no legitimate basis for such a claim, and we strongly suspect that at least in substantial part that would be true of any such claims asserted here. Let me give the Court a specific example in the Blaskic case. In the Blaskic case there were continuing protests that some of the requests were calling for highly sensitive information that touched on national security issues. Ultimately when some of these documents were produced, they were gasoline receipts. They were gasoline receipts. Highly sensitive information. Further, Your Honours, even -- and I stress the word "even" -- where there is some legitimate basis or aspect of a national security concern, it is likewise our experience, and I suspect the Court's experience in its local or domestic jurisdictions as well, it is likewise our experience and assessment that such concerns can very often be addressed in such a way that the documents or information itself can be provided in a way that does no significant injury to any legitimate security interest. The information can be postured in such a way, protective orders can be entered in such a way that assuming that there is any legitimate interest, that interest be protected while making most if not all the information available to the Court. In connection with our application dated the 25th of January, 1999, Your Honour, and this Court's 4 February order for production, we had 38 paragraphs of requests, after litigation in the Appeals Chamber, adverse to Croatia. Some eight months after this court's order, Croatia finally produced three documents. So out of 38 paragraphs, they had documents responsive to only one out of 38 paragraphs and then that one paragraph they produced three documents. We don't accept that that's full compliance. We then, Your Honour, on the 16th of April, 1999, applied for an order, which is pending at this time. There were approximately 41 numbered paragraphs. Paragraphs 1 through 39 asked for documents and information directly related between the defendant Kordic and 12 identified persons, all of whom were significant political/military leaders in Croatia and Herceg-Bosna during the time in question. We believe those are fair, sufficiently specify a specific and relevant request. Paragraphs 40 and 41 request documents concerning awards, medals, commendations, et cetera, giving to Mr. Kordic by the State of Croatia and/or the Herceg-Bosna or HVO government, and we know, Your Honour, or have reason to believe that such awards were made, but no documents have ever been produced on that issue. I would point out to the Court that on that particular order, there was a parallel order -- application to the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina for a similar order, well, identical order asking for the same 41 numbered paragraphs, and this Court found, on 1st of June, 1999, that the Prosecutor's request were, "Specific, relevant, and not unduly onerous." We submit, Your Honour, that that same finding should be made here. The requests are identical. Let me briefly touch on that Croatia has taken the position, in response to that particular application, that some, that some of the requests are repetitive or asked again for some information on requests not previously granted. That is literally true as to some particular aspects of some of the requests, but the requests are far from identical. They were further modified and further, if you will, developed, that they are in many ways different. Further, Your Honour, we would take the position that had Croatia, in fact, made substantial good faith productions in response to such prior requests or even other similar requests, they might come to this Court on stronger ground, but certainly Croatia can claim no prejudice whatsoever when they've never produced a document in any of them on these matters. Finally, Your Honour, on the 19th of July, and this is the last pending application, we asked for -- we again applied for a number of requests. We candidly indicate, Your Honour, that we know that there are, by paragraph numbers, a large number of requests. As we said in our papers and I will say again now, Your Honour, we will ask the Court, it would be instinctive, if the Court will allow me to say, it would be instinctive for the Court to say that's an awful lot of requests, surely too many. We believe it is not, Your Honour, and our application should not be judged merely by the number of paragraphs. In fact, each paragraph is limited to directly relevant issues. We have annexed a set of topics so that it doesn't encompass everything. We do not want Dario Kordic's lunch receipts, but touch only on issues that are relevant to the issues before this Trial Chamber about the conflict in Central Bosnia, about the persecution of Muslims, about the attacks on villages, about killings, all directly relevant to the issues before this Chamber. I think in one response that Croatia made to the Court's scheduling order, if I read it correctly, they largely concede, they may have other objections, but they largely concede that the requests themselves are generally specific and relevant. I think that concludes that part of the status of our applications, Your Honour. The Court must have and in the interests of time, Your Honour, I don't know what might have been more efficient, not to go through the chart, because I thought some of the comments to add to the chart rather than simply -- when I say the chart, I mean the table presented -- I hope the Court finds that helpful and the history I've just given to the Court is largely laid out, at least step-by-step without some of the detail, in the table, but I've attempted to further state our position on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have that table.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just say, I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have told us that you are requesting that a senior official representing Croatia, a member of the government or not, in any event, a member of the senior administration of Croatia should be present, should appear to directly respond as an agent of Croatia. It is normal for a state to be represented by its agent and by legal counsel. Have you made such a request to Croatia and have you been in touch with the government of Croatia already, asking them to designate an appropriate interlocutor in order to discuss with that interlocutor the request of cooperation with the International Tribunal for the provision of information and documents within the framework of a court case, because, after all, in relations with a state, that would appear to be normal conduct throughout the world; that is, contacts with the senior representative of the state when one could ask them to designate an interlocutor who could then discuss those matters with you. Have you done that within the Office of the Prosecutor? If you haven't, do you wish to make a precise request to that effect or are you requiring a ruling to that effect on the part of our Chamber? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The correct answer -- Your Honour, I thank you and a comment, the short answer is no, we have not done that, at least not recently. I think, in fact, over the three years there's been extensive consultation. I am sure that if Mr. Harmon stood up, Mr. Harmon could give you about lengthy discussions -- about discussions and conversations, exchange of correspond with the representatives of the government of Croatia, to shorten some requests, to modify some requests, to make some requests more specific. So, yes, I would say on behalf of the Prosecution office as a whole, since 1997, I would say yes, it has happened, Your Honour. Not recently on behalf of the Kordic specific team, and for the very reason, Your Honour, that given the history in this case of three years, of what we view as non-compliance, did not appear to us it was likely to be productive. We're happy to pursue that, Your Honour, to the extent the Court would wish us to, if it would be productive. But it's our judgement it would not be productive, Your Honour. When orders are issued by this Court, which have been, it seems to us that it is the responsibility of the party receiving the order to fully comply with the Court's order and not up to the Prosecutor to try to talk them into it. There are outstanding orders to them, not subject to us negotiating with them further. And I would also further respond if they wanted to have such a dialogue, Your Honour, they've known where we were for the past three years and the past 18 months, and there has never been a phone call, Your Honour. And, in fact, all the voluntary requests for assistance that we've made, and I pointed out some a few minutes ago, dating a year and a half, two years ago, voluntary requests, not with judicial orders entered, were never responded to. We never got a response; no documents, no letter, just nothing. So, Your Honour, sadly I tell the Court our position is that we don't think, absent this Court's direction, absent this Court's intervention, we don't think such a dialogue would be productive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second part of my question, if I understand you well, you're formally asking our Chamber to order Croatia, the Croatian State, to designate a representative, a senior official, to express himself concerning the existence or nonexistence of those documents, and efforts made within the state administration to find them, in the case that they do not exist, and to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Court is obviously correct. The Court may recall that in a similar hearing some time ago with another party, Mr. Nice had stated, and I think the same statement applies equally here, it is all too easy for a legal -- a lawyer representing a party or a client to come and make generic claims or positions; that because the lawyer himself is not in a position to know the details, the lawyer himself is not perhaps a witness, is not put under oath, there simply is not a great deal of force, unfortunately, in some situations, and in the circumstances, we submit, here, to continue general statements or assurances of production or the lack of documents. When, however, a response -- and I think this is true again from our experience, Your Honour, and I can say, having practised both in the civil and criminal arenas for the past 20 years, that when a responsible party has to raise his or her hand and give some certification subject to the penalties of perjury or contempt, it has a way of focusing one's attention, and when it turns out that those statements or those certifications are not entirely true, some consequences can be visited upon that person. In our experience, Your Honour, in these governments the people who are probably the most directly related to these issues typically seem to be the Ministers of Defence and Justice, so if the Court is asking me to, if you will, nominate some possible officials, those are the first two who would come to mind. Your Honour, I'm going to cut through a number of other things here. Papers speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's right. You make, in the 22nd of December, observations, I shall put it, rather than "allegations", mainly concerned with Mr. Rivkin. Since he's here and able, if necessary, to deal with them, we can read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Partly they depend on newspaper reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- which we can read at paragraph 77 onwards, and 85. What is this paper, The Nationale?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is one of the primary papers -- a nationally-distributed paper in Croatia, perhaps one of the one or two -- my understanding, one of the top two or three papers in the country. I make no general claims of credit worthiness of the media in general, but only to say that these are nationally-reputable papers in Croatia. I say "these." The papers that are the subject of the -- or the producers of the articles. They purport to rely, Your Honour, not simply on what might be called hearsay or rumour but upon, however they may have gotten them -- and I don't speculate on that -- but on the nature of contemporaneous records of meetings and minutes of meetings and memoranda supporting the statements made. I had not, Your Honour, very specifically in preparing my comments yesterday and today, not intended to go in any great detail into those aspects, because they are in the papers. I had understood and was operating on the assumption that these papers had, in fact, been served upon Croatia some time ago. I regret they haven't been or they apparently weren't. There is apparently no reason to believe that they were not served locally on the embassy on or about December 22nd. It's unfortunate as to why they have not perhaps been communicated more broadly. Let me just say, Your Honour, that, well, if the counsel -- I appreciate the Court's concerns, and counsel certainly should have a chance to respond. It may be that if counsel is directed, as the Court already has, to those pages of our papers that they now have and have had at least for some minutes, perhaps they would be in a position to further respond. I don't think I would like to characterise it too --

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour. We do not have those papers. What we have is a summary that was given to us as we walked into the courtroom. We do not have those papers that my colleague is referring to. And as to the service on the embassy, I believe this issue was already addressed earlier by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm told by the registrar that this document was sent on the 28th of December to Mr. Rivkin. Now, whether that is a change that is due to a change in the firm, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: It is not. If I might clarify, Your Honour. My secretary at my old law firm telephoned us as soon as she received it, so it has nothing to do with change in law firms. That document was physically received in Washington at 3.00 p.m. yesterday when all of us were here sitting and preparing for the hearing this morning. In order to vitiate those problems, perhaps we can ask the Prosecutor, as a courtesy in the future, to inform us at least that such a document has been transmitted so we can make appropriate efforts to obtain it. The Prosecutor certainly has faxed us a number of letters in the last few days and knows very well how to reach us. I don't want to impugn in any way the Prosecutor's behaviour in this matter; nor, on the other hand, is it fair to in any way suggest or insinuate that we somehow deliberately avoided receiving this document. Again, as to the embassy, whenever -- well, I don't want to belabour this point, but it would be unnatural for the embassy to be faxing us a 200-page document that the service sheet indicates was sent to us directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Rivkin, you, for your part, perhaps can tell the embassy to let you know if any documents arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: I will do so in the future, and I will-- but again, just to give you an idea, Your Honour, for example, in a different proceeding, in a case of ICJ, precisely because the documents are only served at the embassy because of an indication where the agent is located, the embassy immediately transmits those documents to us. Here, for over two years, we've always been served directly, and it's very regrettable that there was a change regarding the way the registrar transmits though documents. We'll discuss it with them as well. But I would like to suggest very briefly that it's rather unfair for us to try to read those pages now and try to respond to them, but I would certainly like to have an opportunity to do so in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I'm going to suggest is this: that the relevant paragraphs can be pointed out to you now. We will hear the rest of Mr. Scott's submissions. We will then adjourn for our usual break of half an hour. You'll have the opportunity of reading the relevant paragraphs -- there are not many -- and we'll hear your response. It will be a matter for you, how you put it. Of course, if you want more time, we will hear it, but it may be that these are matters you can deal with, at least in outline form, fairly briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I shall try to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The relevant paragraphs, as far as I can see, are paragraphs 77 and 78 and paragraph 85, which deal with two articles which I referred to from the newspaper, and there is reference to a meeting in which you were involved, it's alleged, at paragraphs 95 onwards. I think that covers --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the Court is absolutely correct. Your Honour, let me just respond to this last issue only briefly. First of all, let me assure that on this particular item, on this particular item, there is no insinuation of bad faith by counsel in trying to avoid the service of these papers. I'm not suggesting that. I would point out to the Court that in correspondence received, by all accounts, by counsel and dated the 20th of December, there is reference to these issues being raised, the letter signed by Mr. Nice and faxed to counsel, which puts out a number of these same issues which the Court was copied on, I believe. Yes. Also on the 11th of January, there was a further letter also copied to the Court, by all indications received by counsel -- we have a fax confirmation -- again setting out a number of at least some of these issues and stating specifically -- and this is my last point on this, Your Honour -- but stating specifically, "In reference to the last part of your 30 December letter, we are taken to understand that you've received all of the recent pleadings and correspondence about the binding order matter with Croatia, although we were not aware that you had changed law firms. If you have any questions whether all of such pleadings or correspondence have reached you, please let us know." This is the first we've heard this morning of any problem. We'll certainly try to be fair in our dealings in the future, as we always have been, Your Honour, although I must say we don't undertake any obligations to act on behalf or carry out the responsibilities of the Croatian embassy. Finally, Your Honour, we go on in our papers, from approximately page 31 to approximately page 40 or so, generally with an account of Croatia's lack of cooperation with this Tribunal for the last three years. Again, in the interests of time, I can give the Court assurance I'm not going to go through that in detail. Suffice it to say, Your Honour, these are not the protests of one Mr. Scott or one trial team. Numerous organisations, institutions, responsible officials, are on record for having concluded that Croatia has not, in fact, been responsible or acted properly towards this Tribunal in the last several years. The Council of Europe has made such a finding in April of this year -- excuse me -- April of 1999. President McDonald sent a report to the Security Council on this issue. The Prosecutor has sent a report to the Security Council on this issue. The annual report of this institution, an official U.N. document speaking for this institution, has stated very clearly Croatia's lack of cooperation with this institution. Again, Your Honour, this non-compliance with binding orders is part of a larger picture to obstruct and delay and interfere with the ability of this institution to carry out its international mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's one argument for a position where a party is known to have a document and the other party asks for it, and one way or another a court can be satisfied that there is a refusal to produce a particular document in litigation. But if the party says there are no such documents, what then are the court's powers or, specifically, what are this Court's powers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the answer to that, Your Honour, is similar to the answer that we proposed to the Court again in another proceeding with another entity, which the Court is familiar with, and in reference to my response to Judge Bennouna a few minutes ago. I agree that always presents a difficult situation to any court of any jurisdiction. I think the only steps that can be taken, Your Honour, in that situation is again to require some senior official, not some mere namesake or token but someone who is in a responsible position to have this information, to come before the Court and make some such certification. That's all we can -- the Court is absolutely right. Ultimately, that's all you can do, and if that official is either unintentionally wrong or intentionally misleading the Court, then if that can be later established, then the Court is in a position to do something about it. There may also be the question, Your Honour, of -- and we just raise this again because Mr. Nice raised it in a prior matter, prior hearing -- there may be some questions of certain adverse inferences being drawn from the lack of production. If a state closely identified with a party, with an accused before this Tribunal, is in a position to produce documents and refuses or fails to do so, I think the Court should at least entertain the notion -- we certainly expect no ruling this morning, but we ask the Court -- we think all of us should entertain the notion that it may be appropriate, and I think this was discussed and perhaps implemented in the Blaskic Chamber -- maybe it was only discussed -- but that is that some inference then be drawn. I realise there is some -- the question will be asked, "How can the lack of cooperation or lack of compliance by one entity be laid at the feet of another party?" I recognise -- we recognise the issue, Your Honour. However, when you have -- as we submit is true here for reasons the Court has heard before and which Mr. Nice may touch on further at a further opportunity, when there is such a complete, in our view, identification between the state which supports a Defence, which pays for a Defence, which is intimately related in the conduct of a Defence, has information documents available to it and refuses to produce them, there may be a situation that negative inferences can and should be drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You suggest that we summon officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think, again, that was another part of the Court's question, and I apologise for not answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. What I want to ask you is simply what are our powers to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think under the Blaskic subpoena decision, the Appeals Chamber in October of 1997, the procedure was laid out that the Court can take steps to put the proceedings in such a posture that if the state continues to be ordered to comply, this Chamber -- this Tribunal can then order the state to identify such specific senior officials, that the authorities of that state not only identify such officials but then further direct them to comply. And that if such compliance is then not forthcoming, essentially what the Tribunal jurisprudence says, as I understand it, Your Honour, is that the Court is then in a position to subpoena those individuals in their personal or individual capacity. That's what we would -- that's where we think we would be on that, Your Honour, in terms of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're referring to the Blaskic decision, it would be helpful to have the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to admit I have not read it recently, and I can do that. I will do it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can deal with it after the break. Just refer us to the paragraph that you're relying on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please try to look at the Blaskic case. But if my memory serves me well, I do not think that is precisely what you are telling us. If my memory serves me well, it is a case, when an order is addressed to a state to carry out the decision of the Tribunal, that in that state an individual receives an order to do something and fails to do that, it means that the decision or, rather, an order is addressed to that state and in that state a specific individual who receives instructions to execute something does not do that, at that moment that individual, that person, then is reduced from the position of a representative of a state to the position of a private person, and the Tribunal then can serve the subpoena, and then in an injunction a subpoena may be issued, but only in his capacity as a private person. And if my memory serves me well, and under the reservation that perhaps I'm wrong, this is what happened in the Blaskic case. At the moment, we're not in that particular position. I believe the state needs to be asked expressly to designate a valid interlocutor on behalf of the state to explain which are the steps which then led them to conclude that there were no documents available. Somebody says 3,000 documents or something. That is what -- that is the legal representative of Croatia says that not one of these documents exists, but Croatia tells us -- that is, Croatia makes a distinction between documents it produces itself and documents which come from some other source. And for the latter, for the documents that come from the other source, it says that it cannot say whether it has them or it doesn't have them, and that is yet another nuance in the position of Croatia, because to say or not to say whether such documents exist or do not would be a national state secret. I believe, and I'm stating, and I speak only in my own name, that I believe such a position is unacceptable. One cannot say that because to turn over the text one has to say -- one cannot say that even saying whether one has or doesn't have a document could also be a secret. That is also unacceptable, and I think this is the first stage. I am speaking, as I said, in my own name, but we shall consult us in the Chamber because this is a point which indeed needs to be clarified. And then the third element concerning the -- concerning Croatia's position. It says that if one is to verify whether there are any documents which constitute a national secret, one needs first to know what is -- and this is also a way of non-responding, that it needs to know which are these documents which were mentioned in the Blaskic case; that is, which are acceptable, which are relevant, and so on and so forth. Now, it seems to me that from the requests which the Prosecutor said that Croatia indeed had all the time available to determine what is and what is not a national secret. And if we can use the existing text, perhaps we could say that the first element is that there is no response because something is not a secret but one has to determine what is a secret or, rather, the objection on the national secret has to be developed today, and we have to hear that from Croatia's representative. Now, having said that, evidently it is necessary for Croatia's representative or some representative of Croatia to tell us about this and not only a law firm which will be here and which will give us some legal thesis about the responsibility, but a representative of Croatia to tell us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, we will also have in mind, while you're considering matters, Rule 54 bis, which we haven't referred to yet, and it may be that the respondents can make their submissions on that Rule after the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Casey, I will refer you specifically to 54 bis (F)(i) which requires the state to identify, as far as possible, the basis upon which it claims that its national security interests will be prejudiced. You will have all those matters in mind, of course. It may be helpful to the Trial Chamber if you were to respond to what Judge Bennouna has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: I would be delighted to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. After the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, if there's anything you want to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. If I can respond to Judge Bennouna, and then I think I can conclude my remarks before the recess if the Court allows me. Three very short responses, Your Honour, and Judge Bennouna. You're absolutely correct. My understanding is the same as yours on the rulings under the Blaskic judgement, and you have said it better than I have been able to say it. That official can then be subpoenaed in what the law considers -- some might call of a legal fiction -- in a private capacity, and that is exactly the position that I understand it to be as well. Secondly, I appreciate the Court pointing out something that's in our papers but I had not yet addressed this morning, and that is the distinction Croatia makes in some of its responses between documents produced or generated by Croatia itself, if you will, and by its agents, and documents in its position from third parties. Let me be completely clear. We do not recognise or take any comfort in that distinction. Our request is, and I believe the Court's orders are documents in their possession. And I would have to tell the Court that we are very concerned that documents -- for instance, that once we're in Bosnia, ones possessed by the HVO or ones possessed by the Herceg-Bosna government, have in the ensuing years found their way into Croatia or into the hands of certain parties or organisations or governments in Croatia. So let me be clear. I believe the Court's orders and certainly our requests are for all documents in their possession by whoever initially generated or collected. On the national security issue, Your Honour, the third point, Judge Bennouna, you've raised, again I completely agree with you. There have to be specific steps taken -- and the President was also correct -- under the new Rule 54 bis to be very specific. We think there is a very high burden to meet in justifying and setting out the basis for a national security claim. I agree with Your Honour. Let me just close with this, Your Honour: We believe these issues are of a paramount importance to this Tribunal, not just the Kordic case, not just this Trial Chamber. The ability for this institution and indeed for a future International Criminal Court to conduct its business in an effective way has to provide for a way, a mechanism for courts to enter orders and ensure that those orders are complied with. Otherwise, Your Honour, if you will allow me, we are a paper tiger. We make strong statements that cannot be enforced. I don't think that's the position we should be in. In terms specifically of where we stand, and I close with this, after three years, Your Honour, since January of 1997, here is the score: In the Blaskic case, perhaps something like half or more of a small box of documents produced in three years, most of it unresponsive or irrelevant, continued denials that other documents exist or alleged national security concerns. In the Kordic case specifically, starting in July 1998 with our first request, 31 documents were produced in response to a request and subsequent application for something that we've shorthand termed the "Bobetko documents." We tell the Court that they were not produced voluntarily. In fact, this goes back to a question that, Judge Bennouna, you raised a few minutes ago. We asked for them voluntarily. We never got a response, didn't get a telephone call, didn't get a letter. There was simply no recognition of our request. We waited for some period of time. Some months went by. We then sought -- applied to this Court for an order. The order was issued and the documents were finally produced. And I submit, Your Honour, the only reason, in our view, frankly, that they were produced is because General Bobetko had seen the wisdom of writing a book about the war in which he identified all these orders very specifically, and, quite frankly, Croatia and its representatives were not in a position to deny the existence of the orders. They simply had no alternative essentially but to produce them. Beyond that, Your Honour, we have three documents produced in response to a 34-paragraph request on the Cerkez case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I don't want to interrupt you, but I think we have those points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until half past 11.00, Mr. Casey, and we'll hear you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a request from the interpreters and those who are following in a different language, would the parties slow down in their submissions, please, and have others in mind. Mr. Casey, beginning with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will keep that in mind. May it please the Court, Croatia and the Office of the Prosecutor obviously see the world very differently. In Croatia's view, it has complied with the Court's orders. It has not provided materials to the OTP in response to any of the OTP's requests for assistance because it did not believe that the OTP was legally entitled to those materials. The OTP has asked for things that were framed far too broadly and in many cases it would have required simply turning over the military or other archives of the Croatian government to satisfy them. Croatia contested the legal sufficiency of the OTP's requests for orders, and it prevailed. It is, in fact, the OTP that consistently has refused to accept the Appeals Court's rulings on this matter in October of 1997, and it has continued to demand materials that it is otherwise not legally entitled to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel please down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: This is not non-compliance by Croatia but a refusal by the OTP to accept the legal rulings of the Court. The OTP's claim that the materials produced by Croatia were irrelevant and unresponsive also is misplaced. Given the breadth of the OTP's requests, it is difficult to see how these materials could not have been responsive. It may be more accurate to say that the materials were unhelpful to the OTP's case. However, Croatia's compliance with the Court's orders cannot be judged on the basis of whether it produces materials that support the Office of the Prosecutor's accusations. The complaints of various political institutions that Croatia has failed in its obligations to the International Tribunal are precisely that, complaints by political institutions and not legal opinions. As to the report by former Prosecutor Arbour to the Security Council, that was the opinion of Mrs. Arbour. It was transmitted to the Security Council by President McDonald without legal process because the President believed that the Court's Rules did not provide for a legal process before the transmission was made. Hopefully, that will be changed. However, to characterise the support to the Security Council as the view of the International Tribunal or to give it the character of a judicial determination is entirely wrong. Croatia understands that Mrs. Arbour was not satisfied with its cooperation with her office, but it believes that it fully complied with its legal obligations and that Mrs. Arbour simply was asking for more than she was entitled to. With respect to the question of the appearance of an official of the Republic of Croatia before the Court, the OTP has actually referred to one part of the October 29 decision but, alas, not the portion of that opinion on point. There is no authority in the International Tribunal to require a state official to come before the Tribunal and to, under oath and subject to penalties of perjury or contempt, make statements with respect to that individual's official duties. The relevant paragraph is paragraph 38 of the 29 October 1997 opinion. There the Court stated: "The Appeals Chamber dismisses the possibility of the International Tribunal addressing subpoenas to state officials acting in their official capacity. Such officials are mere instruments of a state, and their official action can only be attributed to the state. They cannot be the subject of sanctions or penalties for conduct that is not private but undertaken on behalf of a state. In other words, state officials cannot suffer the consequences of wrongful acts which are not attributable to them personally but to the state on whose behalf they act. They enjoy so-called functional immunity."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise, but that is too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll go more slowly. "This is a well-established rule of customary international law, going back to the 18th and 19th centuries, restated many times since." The following paragraphs may also be of interest to the Court. I will not read from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Casey, I should like to interrupt you for a moment on this point, because that will perhaps help us to make progress, which is our common purpose, for justice to be served. You are citing the ruling in the Blaskic case. That has to do with the fact of addressing a subpoena to a representative of a state. We cannot do it to a state, nor to a state representative, because they are covered by immunity, as they are acting on behalf of the state. That is quite evident. But that is not the question we are addressing here. We are not talking about a subpoena. You're not responding to the question. The question put is to ask the state to identify a person, a high official, to express himself on behalf of the state, and I think that there is no prohibition on this in international law, as far as we know. There is no impediment to asking a state to designate an agent to tell us what measures have been taken to honour their international obligations on behalf of the state and to come and present the position of the state. So what was in question in Blaskic was the possibility of addressing an order under penalty of sanctions. That is a subpoena, that is what a subpoena means. And it was stated that one could not do that, that one cannot sanction a state, as such, and address a subpoena to a state for the reasons presented in the Blaskic ruling. That is the problem. So will you please respond to the question that has been raised, and we will be very appreciative of your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree, Your Honour, that the International Tribunal is entirely entitled to request that a state designate an official to travel here to explain to the Court what measures it has taken to comply with the Court's orders. What I was responding to was the suggestion by the Prosecutor that that individual, when they came, would be put under oath and would be subject to penalties of perjury and perhaps to contempt. It is only that that I believe, both under the October ruling and international law generally, that cannot be done. The Court clearly can request that the state designate an individual and request that that individual come to explain its position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to the issue of national security, under Rule 54 bis it is incumbent upon a state to bring to the Court's attention, as specifically as it can, national security objections to an application within five days before a hearing. On January 7th, Croatia filed a response to the Court's scheduling order and a request or application for an extension of time to make further national security objections. The objections stated in the January 7th filing were admittedly broad, but they were as specific as possible, given the nature of the Prosecutor's categorical requests. Now, it is obviously the case that depending on the request, whether it be for a specific document or specific category or set of documents, one may well be able to tell, from the face of the request, that there are specific national security objections to the production of the documents. At the same time, it may not be possible to tell that, to a categorical request, until all the documents that might be responsive to that category have been collected and identified and the appropriate officials have had the opportunity to determine whether production of any particular document would comprise the country's national security. I think Judge Bennouna referred to the question of third-party documents and whether a state can merely assert that because a request calls for third-party documents, that its national security is implicated and therefore it does not have to produce the documents. Croatia has never asserted so much. Croatia's position is that with respect to third-party documents in individual cases, it may well compromise its national security to admit that it is in possession of such documents, because to do that could reveal how it obtained the documents and could well reveal sources and methods of intelligence gathering, a matter that all states consider a matter of vital national security. Again, it is impossible to say, at least with the requests in the Prosecutor's July 19 application, as well as the April 16 application, whether that will be a problem with any specific document. That will not be -- Croatia will not be able to determine that until it identifies any documents that are responsible to the orders. Now, it is also true that at least with respect to the April 16th application, Croatia has been in possession of that application for some time. With respect to the July 19th application, the country, as I understand, received that only after the Court issued its December 15 order. I believe -- I hope they received it in advance of when we did, but -- and so they've had that much less time. However, the Prosecutor has consistently maintained that merely because the Prosecutor applies for an order, the state is immediately required to begin collecting documents as if it were to respond or comply with that order before the order has even been issued by the Trial Chamber. If due process is to have any meaning at all, the state cannot be required to begin complying with one of the Prosecutor's requests until after the Court has issued a proper legal order, assuring itself that the requirements set out in the October 27, 1997 opinion, as glossed by the September 9, 1999 opinion in the Cerkez case, have been met. Therefore, Croatia has asked for and believes that it will need the additional time it has asked for, 45 days from the time an order actually issues by the Court, to identify further national security objections, and ultimately 60 days to produce whatever it may have that is responsive to the Court's order. Croatia believes that that is an entirely reasonable period of time, and indeed it is only 15 days more than the original 45 days the Prosecutor itself suggested in the 19 July application. Finally, before I turn the podium over to Mr. Rivkin to discuss the issues that were raised in the Prosecutor's submission, one point on the issue that the Prosecutor has raised of the alleged support by the Republic of Croatia for the Defence in the Kordic case, I would simply point out that it is no more inappropriate for a state to render assistance to the Defence, or the lawyers for that state, for that matter, assuming that they are within the bounds of any orders the Court has issued, as it is for states to offer assistance to the Office of the Prosecutor, which we believe has also been the case. Indeed, I would point out that of the lawyers standing here today, four of us have, at various times, served in the United States Department of Justice; Mr. Rivkin, myself, Mr. Harmon, and Mr. Scott. And I believe at least at one point lawyers were seconded or detailed from the Department to assist the Office of the Prosecutor. I think it is important to keep in mind that merely because the Office of the Prosecutor has brought allegations against individuals, allegations which we must all accept as nothing more than allegations until the Prosecutor has proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt here in court, it has not, by that act, lined up the entire world against the defendant. It is not the world versus the defendant, it is not the United Nations versus the defendant, it is not right-thinking states versus the defendant, it is merely the Prosecutor versus the defendant, and it is up to the Court to determine, ultimately, whether there is guilt or innocence. So states are perfectly free, and properly, to give assistance to either the Prosecutor or the defendant as they may see fit, within the bounds of their international obligations, and we believe that Croatia has fully complied with those limits. Thank you, Your Honour. I would be happy to answer any questions the Court may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Casey, just this: I referred you to Rule 54 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now that, in relation to national security interests under Subrule (F)(i), requires the state to identify, as far as possible, the basis upon which a national security interest is claimed. Now, I anticipate that to mean more than merely an assertion, that what will be required is the identification, at least in general terms, of what the interest is. It will not be sufficient merely to say a national security interest is involved. It will be necessary for the state to go further than this, and it may be by the calling of evidence to establish what that interest is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would -- we understand that, Your Honour. I believe in the January 7th submission, that Croatia identified the basis of its interests as far as possible at this time, that being two; that the April 16th order requests certain documents from and to the then President of Croatia as well as its Defence Minister. The correspondence of the head of state as well as the head of the country's military normally is considered to be of national security concern. Again, it may not be that all of the correspondence is. You can only determine that on a document-by-document basis. But that is one of the bases upon which Croatia has a national or may have a national security concern with some of the documents once it reviews whatever it may have in its possession. The second basis was the third-party issue, and that is many or most of the requests in the April 16th, as well as in the July 19th applications, seek documents that were not generated or at least presumably not generated in Croatia or by Croatian government officials. Mostly they seek documents either from or to the defendant Mr. Kordic and various other named individuals. Consequently, if Croatia is in possession of some or all of those documents, how it came into possession of those documents might well raise a national security interest. Again, the basis would be that it would reveal the sources and methods of intelligence gathering or even intelligence capabilities. I mean if you don't have a document, it may reveal as much about your intelligence capabilities as if you do. Again, because of the categorical nature of requests, Croatia cannot be more specific at this time until specific documents have been identified and a review of them can be made. Indeed, even once a review is made whether to assert a national security interest, should it exist, is a matter for the elected government to determine. So again, Croatia's requested some additional time so that process can take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Judge May, Judge Bennouna, I will try very briefly to respond to several points made by the OTP in their written submission. Indeed, I'm grateful to Judge May for bringing them to my attention. I, of course, have not had much time to study them so would like perhaps to reserve an opportunity to respond to them -- I better slow down -- to respond to them in writing at the earliest possible opportunity, but I certainly am able to make a couple of preliminary observations, because I think those points are not very difficult to respond to. Number one, I notice that the particular numbered paragraphs that Judge May referred to cite newspaper articles. If I'm not mistaken, fairly recently in this very Trial Chamber, in response to a controversy involving the issue of withdrawal of Tribunal funding for the lawyers in the Kupreskic case that was undertaken by the registrar, and I apologise if I have the Trial Chamber wrong, has pointed out that newspaper articles are inherently unreliable methods of -- a means of proving any point. Indeed, I would mention that there are a number of newspaper articles, not only in Croatian newspapers but papers like the New York Times, one of the most respected newspapers in the world, that have made allegations, for example, arguing, for example, that the OTP has leaked information about alleged indictments against President Tudjman, prompting OTP to respond that this is not the case. So newspapers quite often get their facts wrong. That's sort of the first point. The second point: It's always difficult for counsel to respond to newspaper accounts or any other accounts that involve confidential the attorney/client privilege which is certainly very important to any of us who practice law and one of the most important means of ensuring due process and liberty. However, I think in this case my situation is somewhat easier, because I can point out that as the Prosecutor very well knows, those newspaper accounts actually deal with an entirely different matter. Again, if you actually read those newspaper accounts, the way the Prosecutor weaves the facts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: The way the Prosecutor weaves the facts in those numbered paragraphs would lead one to believe that the subject matter involved was the general strategy of Croatia vis-a-vis this Court or, rather, the way the Prosecutor categorises the general strategy of non-compliance or obstruction by Croatia vis-a-vis this Court. Actually, those articles deal solely with one issue and one issue only, which is the position of Croatia regarding the question of whether or not this Tribunal has jurisdiction over operations storm and flash. It has nothing to do with Blaskic case, Kordic case, production of documents in any of those cases. And again, while I'm constrained by the bounds of attorney/client privilege from getting in a lot of detail, I can certainly tell Your Honours, and I believe some of Your Honours know that from other context that the Croatian position was, is, and remains that this Tribunal lacks jurisdiction over those particular operations and that this matter should be resolved for a judicial process. And I should hasten to add that Croatia has pointed out consistently in writing and orally that it would be bound by whatever decision is reached by this Tribunal, judicial decision is reached by this Tribunal regarding these operations. So I am really puzzled as to why those articles are being trotted out on the issue of what has Croatia's record or strategy been relative to production of documents. Let me now just briefly make another point in this regard; that it has never been the position of the Republic of Croatia to adopt a general strategy of non-cooperation with the Tribunal. That strategy has never been, to the best of my knowledge, discussed, raised, or communicated in any meeting or encounter in which we have -- that has taken place. Have we ever heard such a strategy even being discussed, again, a generic strategy of non-compliance with Croatia's legal obligations? We have advised our client, in the strongest possible terms, not to do so because indeed that would have been in violation of international legal obligations and Article 29 and perhaps other bases in other international law. And lastly, on that point, I am enormously disappointed in the fact that the OTP continues to -- and I say continues because we had an exchange of correspondence in this matter that I hope perhaps erroneously closed this issue down to mischaracterise, which is rather unusual for especially people trained in Anglo-Saxon law, mischaracterised position, or I should say relationship between counsel and the client. It is never the case. I've already mentioned to Your Honours what has been the position of Republic of Croatia regarding cooperation of the Tribunal.
