But in any case, it has never been the role of counsel, in this or any other representation to decide policy for its client, be it Republic of Croatia, a corporation, an individual. What we have always done and will continue to do for this or any other client, and any lawyer I know of serving in the legal capacity, is to tell the client what its legal options are. It is the client's choice what policy to adopt, but it is incumbent upon any lawyer to the extent that there are valid legal arguments which go to the question of what precisely a client's obligation is, to advise the client as to what legal options they have. If you don't, indeed I would argue that in most circumstances you would be committing malpractice, but it's always the client's decision as to what policy to adopt. And the last point I would like to make, and I'm supplementing an observation made by my distinguished colleague, Mr. Casey, relative to Croatia's interest in cooperating with various defendants, in addition to everything that Mr. Casey has said, I would like to point out that obviously a great deal of interest on Croatia's part in what is happening in these cases is attributable precisely to the fact that the OTP chose to prosecute these individuals not merely for specific acts or activities but in the process as indeed -- not inappropriate, sought to paint a picture of actions by the Republic of Croatia during certain portions of a conflict following the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia, that, from the position of Republic of Croatia, are completely untrue and unfair. And the Republic of Croatia indeed is in a difficult position or any other sovereign state. It is not a party, it is not able to come in and directly argue on the question of whether or not, for example, there was an armed conflict in Central Bosnia. It doesn't -- indeed, I think at one point the Republic of Croatia has asked for an opportunity to even submit an affidavit on that point in Kordic case and I believe, if my memory serves me -- Blaskic case, forgive me. If my memory serves me right, the problem was that it was rather late in the trial, but also it wasn't obvious what would be the probable value of such a memorial given any status of a state like Croatia or states like Croatia vis-a-vis this Tribunal. And it's quite natural, as I said, in addition to what my colleague, Mr. Casey, said, it's quite natural for a state in a proceeding or proceedings where it feels its behaviour in the past is being quite unfairly characterised to be actively working with those parties who do have an opportunity to say something in the courtroom. It would be foolhardy. I cannot see any other sovereign state acting in that fashion. So to me, as long as everybody is operating within the bounds of protective orders and that certainly has been the case, I can't imagine how anybody would try to base any imputation or inference of conduct, good or bad for the defendant or for the state involved, from those exchanges. Thank you, Your Honours. I would be happy to respond to it in writing, indeed I will at greater length, but that's what I wanted to say today. I would be happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question but, rather, for Mr. Casey, regarding his comment concerning the interpretation of Rule 54 bis. This Rule relating to orders to states for the production of documents has the following form: The criteria are indicated for issuing such an order. I don't know whether Croatia is contesting that those criteria are stipulated, that the documents be identified, that they are relevant, that there was an attempt made to obtain them by other means, through cooperation and so on. Then also there is the possibility for the Judges rejecting that request, and that is not under (B). Then we come to (C); that is the possibility of appeal. And under (D), that applies to us, and that is that we decide to hear the state in audience, and such a hearing was decided and envisaged for today, the 13th of January. We are in the situation envisaged under (D), and we come to the situation under (E), which doesn't concern us. It doesn't concern us. What does concern us is the (D) and the (F). Do we agree on that? Under (F) it is stated that prior to the hearing, a state may make an objection claiming national security interest. And, as you say, the basis for such an objection, the grounds, have to be provided, specified, as is stated under (F). Then if an objection is made, which you appear to be doing, we either ask you to explain yourself clearly or to require a special hearing to hear your objection, which is something that you haven't done. So what are you telling us, make the decisions first and then we shall see? But that is not what is envisaged under Article 54 bis. It doesn't function in that way at all. It does not oblige us to make a ruling and depending on that ruling, because you made an interpretation which is not correct. It is clear from this Rule, which says that if you have an objection, you can present it now, which do you not wish to do, or you can require protective measures for your objection to be protected to the maximum as well as national security interests, and after the Court, the Chamber has heard you, it is only then that we make our ruling, taking into consideration the criteria, which we don't know if you are contesting them or not because you haven't said anything, and taking into consideration the national security interests. Therefore, we wish to draw your attention to the fact we cannot, as you are saying, make a ruling and give you 45 days to respond regarding national security interests and then give you 60 days after that. It doesn't work that way. Therefore, if you have an objection based on national security interests, you must make it, and if you wish it to be protected, you must request a hearing implementing Article 54, and it provides certain guarantees under (F). If you don't do that, that means that the Tribunal will go over your objection, that it has no contents. It is up to you to give it substance. You must request a hearing, and it is up to us to decide whether we will grant it to you, providing guarantees and necessary protections. That is what I'm trying to say, that your interpretation of Rule 54 is not a good one. It doesn't function that way. It is not up to us to make a ruling and then to give you an opportunity to see whether the documents we are requesting can be claimed national security interests. We do not first have to say which are the documents corresponding to the criteria and then you will see whether you will object or not. That is not what is stipulated. I apologise for drawing your attention to this. Normally it is up to you to tell us, according to the Rules of the Tribunal, whether you have an objection concerning national security interests, if you wish to present it. And if you're asking for a hearing with protective guarantees, it is up to the Tribunal to respond, the hearing will be held, and the Trial Chamber will decide on the order to be issued concerning the production of documents. That is what is stipulated in the text. I wanted to tell you this. I don't know whether you have any comments, but I think you have to react, because if you don't react, then it is our understanding that you have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would like the opportunity to react. I understand the interpretation of the Rule that Your Honour has outlined. As to the elements of Rule 54 bis, they appear to restate the tests, the requirements adopted by the Appellate Chamber in the 29 October, 1997 judgement, and Croatia has no objection to those elements. It is true that the Rule is crafted in such a way that one would expect a state to make its national security objections five days before a hearing. However, the Rule does state that the state need only identify those as far as possible, and what Croatia has said is that looking at the requests from the Prosecutor, it is impossible to tell, from the face of the requests, all of the potential national security objections that it may have. From the face of the requests, it can see that some types of documents that have been requested are likely to cause a national security problem if they are released, and Croatia stated in the January 7th submission the basis of those concerns. It also, at that time, asked the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is a very simple one. You have a request for the production of documents. You have a principled objection claiming national security interests. We are agreed. You have a submission a week prior to the hearing. It is up to you now to tell us whether, yes or no, you wish to present in detail and within which deadline those national security objections and under which guarantees. It is up to you to tell us. If you don't tell us, you cannot seek shelter by saying a priori in a general manner, "We cannot tell," and so on. That's very vague. It's up to you to be specific. That is envisaged by the rule. Are you asking for a hearing to present your national security objections or not? If you are not, then we will rely on your filings which simply -- your submission, which simply says that there may be national security interests. It is up to you to tell us whether you want a hearing or not. If you are not requesting a hearing, there is no national security objection. That is the text and that is what I'm asking you to consider. We are not going to take a decision on the production of documents and give you, after that, 45 days. That is not what is envisaged by the Rule. The Rule says if you have an objection and if you want guarantees, you ask for a hearing and you present your objections. I'm asking you to tell us clearly: Are you here to speak on behalf of Croatia? As a professional lawyer, you must respond to a legal text as it stands. You may need instructions from the state that employs you. It's up to you to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What Croatia requested was not a hearing, admittedly, but it was the practical equivalent of that, which is additional time to make more specific objections. Whether it would make sense to have those objections done in a hearing context, it may well be most efficient and useful for the Court to have a hearing at which an official appears to articulate more specifically the national security objections. At the same time, it may be that once documents have been collected and reviewed, there will be no national security objection or, if there is, the state will decide, as a matter of policy, not to assert it but to surrender the documents in any case. It is really only the elect representatives of the state that can decide how to handle that. I agree with Your Honour that the Rule appears to contemplate that all national security objections will be made by five days before the hearing. And in some cases that may work very well, because it will be obvious what documents are called for and what documents the state has and what the national security objection is. What I'm saying is that here that is not the case. Therefore, we have requested the Court essentially to grant us an extension of time to make those objections. Again, I believe the Court fully has the authority to do that, both under Rule 54 and under Rule 127 if it is disposed to do that. I would like to make clear that we have not asked for 45 days to make national security objections and then an additional 60 days to produce the documents. What we have asked for, effectively, is 60 days to produce the documents but within that period to be able to raise, within 45 days, if some of the documents -- if release of some of the documents would cause a national security problem, to be able to bring that to the Court's attention. It may well be that a hearing would be the best way to do that, assuming there are such additional objections. My colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Casey. Is there anything else you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but my colleague Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RIVKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just a factual observation. We fully appreciate that in the normal course of things, of course, the interpretation advanced by His Honour Judge Bennouna would, indeed, be operational, which is to say the state would collect the documents, the relevant -- identify all responsive documents, would look at them, analyse them, and make a decision as to whether or not to assert national security objections. We beg Your Honours' indulgence. It's somewhat of an unusual time. Croatia is, of course, a sovereign state and continues to function during the transition period, as indeed other countries. But as a practical matters, I hope Your Honours would not be too displeased with the observation that this is, from a bureaucratic perspective, a somewhat different situation than we had, let's say, three months ago or would have again three months from now, which is the ability to get very senior people to focus on the issues is somewhat limited. It is for that reason and that reason only we're proceeding in this manner, and one thing we certainly wish to avoid is to make a request for a national security hearing in a situation that it's quite possible that the relevant government officials, once they complete the collection of responsive documents and analyse them, would decide not to make such an objection. I believe Croatia takes those matters quite seriously, so we didn't want to ask, without a compelling reason, for such a hearing. Again, I want to assure Your Honours this is not -- no disrespect is intended here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Mr. Nice, I don't know that any reply is called for. If there is any matter you want to deal with shortly, in terms of clarification, if you would be short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll be short and, I hope, to the point. First, presumably a responsible government, on receipt of the applications, will have identified the documents, for only by identifying the documents can it know what its response should be, particularly its response in relation to national security concerns. These applications range between January and July of last year. Therefore, there has already been six months for the preparation of documents, as must have taken place for this matter to be dealt with responsibly, and identification of whether there are any national security concerns to be raised. Accordingly, there is no need for further time. I remind the Chamber, particularly in light of the last observation by Mr. Rivkin, that in, I think, April of last year -- it may be this ought to be in private session, it's paragraph 45 -- it's May of last year, paragraph 45 -- to deal with it without needing to go into private session, I just say this: Time was taken with the forecast of exactly such a hearing, the time having been taken, delay having been bought. The hearing was then abandoned. Many of these matters have already been litigated, insofar as they have been in Blaskic, and accordingly preparation as to how to deal with the documents was made by the state then, years ago. That's all that needs to be said about national security. The breadth of the orders were only appealed in one of the Cerkez orders. That appeal was rejected. The vulnerability of an individual to sanctions is dealt with at paragraph 51 of the Blaskic decision. I needn't go through it. I know that the Chamber is familiar with those passages. It's a question of fact. I observe, dealing with the overall arguments raised about cooperation in the Kordic Defence and also in relation to the newspaper articles and the meeting that occurred between all the lawyers and other representatives, I observe that there's no challenge to the accuracy of what's said there. The newspaper articles proceed, for the large part, on the basis of minutes, the accuracy of which is not challenged. They are generic in many places in what they describe of the advice given and the response taken by the state of Croatia. Such phrases as "dragging its feet" will be familiar to the Chamber from its reading of the papers. The matter is adequately pleaded and is in no way met. May we please have a private session for one short matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can only invite Your Honours today to suggest to the Defence this: that in the same way as it might have been wise and appropriate to prepare documents on receipt of applications in order to know what they were to deal with them, rather than to put it off to hearing dates, that it might now be wise for them to prepare against the orders, if any, made when Judge Robinson makes the Court fully composed. It might be wise to prepare for them on that basis, because this Tribunal might think that it could give very abbreviated time scales to reflect the ability of Croatia to use the intervening time for those purposes. The time scales proposed by Croatia would, of course, take any production beyond the end of the Prosecution case in Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it will be very brief and only on any new point. We don't want to hear any more argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would point out that with respect to the 19 July submission, Croatia has only had that since December, and it is very voluminous. Moreover, it is not the case that one must collect all the documents to respond to an order with objections if, on the face of the order, it does not meet the requirements for specificity, relevance, burden, and that kind thing, and so the Prosecution is going from an improper premise. I would also like to respond to what the Prosecution has said with respect to the remarks of Mr. Smith, and perhaps we should be in closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: It will only take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Casey, we have litigated this matter thoroughly. If there's anything you want to add to what Mr. Rivkin is going to say in writing, you can say it, but I think we've heard enough on this topic. Both sides have aired their views.

utterances.speaker: MR. CASEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider this matter, and we shall make our order when the Trial Chamber is fully composed. The parties will be informed in writing. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: concluded at 12.36 p.m.
